zh: 取走卡牌只会让一圈卡变少，不会改变剩余卡的循环相对顺序；而把目标转到队首只有两个方向：从前往后挪，或从后往前挪。
设当前所有剩余卡面值之和为 T，从队首顺时针到目标之前那些卡的面值和为 L：一直把队首移到队尾的代价是 L，一直把队尾移到队首（包括目标自己）的代价是 T−L，每一轮取两者较小值即可，且两种方式取走目标后剩余序列完全相同。
用以原下标为位置的树状数组维护尚未取走的卡面值；维护队首游标 head（目标原下标加一，越界回到 1）；对 k=1..n，用至多两段前缀和求出 L（目标在 head 之前时加上 T 表示绕一圈），答案累加 min(L,T−L)，再在树状数组中把该位置减去 k、T 减去 k；全程用 64 位整数比较和累加，最后才对 1000000007 取模。
en: Taking a card out only shrinks the circle; it never changes the cyclic order of the remaining cards. And there are only two ways to bring the target to the front: move cards from the front to the back, or from the back to the front.

Let T be the sum of all remaining face values and L the sum of the cards from the front, going forward, up to just before the target: moving the front card to the back repeatedly costs L, and moving the back card to the front repeatedly (including the target itself) costs T - L; take the smaller of the two each round, and both ways leave exactly the same sequence after the target is extracted.

Keep a Fenwick tree over the original positions holding the face values of cards not yet taken, and a front cursor head (the target's original index plus one, wrapping to 1); for k = 1..n compute L from at most two prefix sums (add T when the target lies before head, meaning a wrap-around), add min(L, T - L) to the answer, subtract k at that position in the tree and from T; compare and add with 64-bit integers throughout and take the result modulo 1000000007 only at the end.

explanationEn:
## Source and conventions

fastprep/infosys/infosys-extract-cards.md in the pinned commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc gives the full original bounds: 1≤n≤100000, and cards is a permutation of 1 to n. You may move the front card to the back or the back card to the front, each costing the value of the moved card, and extract 1, 2, …, n in turn for free. The shorthand for the third operation does not repeat the word "front", but the full original example explicitly says "remove the 1st card", and step by step it first moves the target to the front and then extracts it. Based on this complete description of the operation, this site states explicitly that only the current front card can be extracted; removing a target directly from the middle or the back is not allowed. If free extraction from any position were allowed, the original example would need no rotation and would cost 0; if the rule were only relaxed to allow free extraction from both ends, then following the original example's operations costs 11 to extract 1, 2 and 3, after which the remaining [5,4] lets 4 be extracted from the back for free and then 5 for free, for a total of at most 11. Neither relaxed rule matches the original example's answer of 15. This is a reconstruction from the source, not a rule guessed from the curated code. The standard input/output is arranged by this site; only one original example is kept, and the other two public examples are explicitly this site's additions. No upstream code was executed.

## Approach

Removals only reduce the cards on the circle and do not change their relative cyclic order. When handling target k, let L be the sum of the face values of the cards going clockwise from the current front up to just before k, and let T be the current total. Moving the front card to the back one card at a time costs L; moving cards from the back to the front one at a time until k reaches the front costs T−L, and this direction includes the cost of the target k itself. Choose the smaller of the two, then remove k. Whichever direction is chosen, after the removal the front card is k's cyclic successor.

Use a Fenwick tree over the original indices to maintain the sum of the face values of the cards not yet removed. A cyclic range is split into at most two prefix sums; removing k means subtracting k at its original index. There is no need to actually look for the next surviving index: put the front cursor at k's original index plus one; removed positions are 0 in the Fenwick tree, so the following cyclic order is still represented correctly.

## Proof of correctness

Fix the set of remaining cards before one extraction. All rotation states form a cycle; each legal rotation moves between adjacent states, at a cost equal to the face value of the moved card. The shortest route that brings k to the front contains no repeated state: deleting a positive-cost closed walk between repeated states only lowers the cost. So the shortest route must be one of the two simple directions. The forward route moves the cards before k, costing L; the backward route moves the other segment, including k, costing T−L. If k is already at the front, the forward cost is 0, which the formula still covers.

Both routes end with exactly the same linear sequence, whose front is k, and the remaining cyclic order is unchanged. After k is extracted, the rest of the problem is therefore independent of the chosen direction. Taking min(L,T−L) at each stage is achievable and is no greater than the cost of that stage in any legal plan. By induction over the successive extraction stages, the resulting total cost is the global minimum.

The Fenwick tree starts with the original face values, and a removal only reduces that index to 0, so every range sum always equals exactly the sum of the face values of the remaining cards. Empty positions skipped by the front cursor have weight 0 and do not change L. Hence the implementation computes exactly the optimal cost described above.

## Complexity and integers

Building the Fenwick tree takes O(n), the n queries and removals take O(n log n) in total, and space is O(n). All costs are compared and added as unreduced integers, and the result is taken modulo 1000000007 only at the end; the two routes must not be reduced modulo before being compared. The total cost does not exceed n·n(n+1)/2 < 5.1×10^14, so 64-bit signed integers are enough, and Python integers are also safe.

## Independent verification and boundaries

The small-scale oracle runs Dijkstra on the full linear card sequence: it enumerates one front-to-back move, one back-to-front move, and a free extraction only when the front card is the next target, until the sequence is empty. It does not use the cyclic range formula or a Fenwick tree. All 163 unique inputs pass through a real subprocess of the reference program.

The full n=100000 stress tests include ascending order, descending order, and several cut points of the ascending circle. Ascending order costs 0. In descending order each step moves the target at the back to the front, and the last card needs no move, so the exact unreduced cost is n(n−1)/2. For the rotated ascending order [k+1,…,n,1,…,k], only extracting 1 needs moves, costing min(k(k+1)/2, n(n+1)/2−k(k+1)/2), and everything afterwards is free. A random permutation at the maximum size is additionally checked with a block list that maintains the real sequence: it walks the face-value sums of the blocks from both ends, removes the target and resets the front, without using the Fenwick implementation. Two wrong algorithms must exit normally and be rejected by the formal test cases.
